```{r setup}
library(adlaplace)
library(adlaplaceFem)
library(Matrix)
```

# The term

The FEM Matérn prior on the spline weights contributes two terms to the joint
log-density (see `vignette("fem_joint_density")`): a quadratic form,
`random_fem_ssq_*`, and a log-determinant, `random_fem_det_*`. This vignette is
about the first,

$$
f(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\theta)
= -\tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\gamma^\top \mathbf{Q}(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\boldsymbol\gamma ,
$$

where $\boldsymbol\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^n$ holds the spline weights (the random
effects, one per active basis function) and $\boldsymbol\theta=(\mathrm{range},
\mathrm{sd})$, optionally on the log scale.

Splitting the Gaussian log-density this way matters because the two halves have
opposite cost profiles. The quadratic form is arithmetically trivial but
involves all $n$ weights, so its Hessian is an $n\times n$ sparse block. The
log-determinant needs a sparse factorization but depends on $\boldsymbol\theta$
alone, so its Hessian is $2\times2$. `adlaplaceFem` therefore handles them by
different mechanisms: the determinant is a CppAD atomic operation
(`src/fem_logdet_atomic.hpp`), while the quadratic form bypasses the tape
entirely with closed-form derivatives (`src/fem_ssq_analytic.hpp` and
`src/fem_ssq_shard.hpp`). The last section explains why the split falls that
way.

# Structure that makes closed forms possible

Two facts about this term do all the work.

**1. $\mathbf{Q}$ is a linear combination of constant matrices.** The
SPDE precision assembles as

$$
\mathbf{Q}(\boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_j(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\mathbf{M}_j ,
\qquad
\mathbf{M} = \begin{cases}
(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}_2) & \alpha=2,\ m=3,\\
(\mathbf{C},\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}_2,\mathbf{G}_3) & \alpha=3,\ m=4.
\end{cases}
$$

The Gram matrices are fixed once the basis is chosen; they carry no
$\boldsymbol\theta$ dependence at all. Every hyperparameter enters through
$m = 3$ or $4$ scalars.

**2. $f$ is quadratic in $\boldsymbol\gamma$.** So the $\boldsymbol\gamma$
Hessian block is constant in $\boldsymbol\gamma$, and third derivatives in
$\boldsymbol\gamma$ alone vanish.

Together these mean every derivative the Laplace approximation needs is a
handful of $O(\mathrm{nnz}(\mathbf{Q}))$ passes over arrays that are already in
memory.

# The coefficient map

With $\nu = \alpha - 1$ in two dimensions, the public $(\mathrm{range},
\mathrm{sd})$ pair converts to the SPDE parameters as

$$
\kappa = \frac{\sqrt{8\nu}}{\mathrm{range}},
\qquad
\tau = \begin{cases}
\bigl(\kappa\,\sigma\sqrt{4\pi}\bigr)^{-1} & \alpha=2,\\[2pt]
\bigl(\kappa^2\sigma\sqrt{8\pi}\bigr)^{-1} & \alpha=3,
\end{cases}
\qquad \sigma = \mathrm{sd},
$$

so that `sd` is the marginal standard deviation of the field
(`vignette("fem_matern_methods")` derives this). The coefficients are then

| $\alpha$ | $\mathbf{Q}$ | $\mathbf{c}(\boldsymbol\theta)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $\tau^2(\kappa^4\mathbf{C} + 2\kappa^2\mathbf{G} + \mathbf{G}_2)$ | $\tau^2(\kappa^4,\ 2\kappa^2,\ 1)$ |
| 3 | $\tau^2(\kappa^6\mathbf{C} + 3\kappa^4\mathbf{G} + 3\kappa^2\mathbf{G}_2 + \mathbf{G}_3)$ | $\tau^2(\kappa^6,\ 3\kappa^4,\ 3\kappa^2,\ 1)$ |

There is exactly one definition of this map in the package,
`fem_Q_coefficients<Alpha>()` in `src/ad_pack_random_fem.cpp`, and three
consumers go through it: the AD quadratic form, the log-determinant atomic, and
the analytic shard's coefficient tape. Keeping it single-sourced is deliberate —
the three would otherwise drift apart silently, and a mismatch between the
determinant's $\mathbf{Q}$ and the quadratic form's $\mathbf{Q}$ produces a
plausible-looking but wrong likelihood.

# The derivatives

Write $q_j = \boldsymbol\gamma^\top\mathbf{M}_j\boldsymbol\gamma$, so that
$f = -\tfrac12\sum_j c_j q_j$. Everything follows by the product rule, since the
$\mathbf{M}_j$ are constant.

| Block | Closed form |
|---|---|
| $\partial f/\partial\boldsymbol\gamma$ | $-\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\gamma$ |
| $\partial f/\partial\theta_k$ | $-\tfrac12\sum_j \dfrac{\partial c_j}{\partial\theta_k}\,q_j$ |
| $\partial^2 f/\partial\boldsymbol\gamma\,\partial\boldsymbol\gamma^\top$ | $-\mathbf{Q}$ |
| $\partial^2 f/\partial\boldsymbol\gamma\,\partial\theta_k$ | $-\bigl(\partial\mathbf{Q}/\partial\theta_k\bigr)\boldsymbol\gamma$ |
| $\partial^2 f/\partial\theta_k\,\partial\theta_l$ | $-\tfrac12\sum_j \dfrac{\partial^2 c_j}{\partial\theta_k\partial\theta_l}\,q_j$ |

with $\partial\mathbf{Q}/\partial\theta_k = \sum_j (\partial c_j/\partial\theta_k)\mathbf{M}_j$,
another linear combination over the same sparsity pattern.

The third row is the one that pays for the whole design. The
$\boldsymbol\gamma$-$\boldsymbol\gamma$ Hessian block **is the precision matrix
itself**, up to sign, and it does not depend on $\boldsymbol\gamma$. Once
$\mathbf{Q}$ has been assembled for the current $\boldsymbol\theta$ — which the
value and gradient already require — the Hessian block needs no further
arithmetic, just a copy with a sign flip. Note also that only $q_j$ couples to
$\boldsymbol\gamma$ in the two $\boldsymbol\theta$ rows, so the $m$ scalars
$q_j$ are the only $\boldsymbol\gamma$-dependent quantities needed there.

# The third-order term

The Laplace approximation's derivative needs more than the Hessian. Correcting
$\tfrac12\log\det\mathbf{H}$ for the movement of the inner mode requires
$\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^{-1}\partial\mathbf{H}/\partial\theta_k)$, which
`adlaplace` obtains through the `trace_hinv_t` shard method: for each column
$\mathbf{v}$ of a factor of $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$, accumulate the third derivative
of the log-density contracted twice with $\mathbf{v}$.

It is tempting to say the third derivative of a quadratic form is zero, but that
is only true of the $\boldsymbol\gamma\boldsymbol\gamma\boldsymbol\gamma$ block.
The mixed block is not zero, and it is the entire answer:

$$
\frac{\partial^3 f}{\partial\theta_k\,\partial\boldsymbol\gamma\,\partial\boldsymbol\gamma^\top}
= -\frac{\partial\mathbf{Q}}{\partial\theta_k}.
$$

The directions `adlaplace` supplies are scattered into $\boldsymbol\gamma$ slots
only, so $\mathbf{v}_{\boldsymbol\theta}=\mathbf{0}$. The order-2 Taylor
coefficient of $f$ along such a direction is
$-\tfrac12\mathbf{v}^\top\mathbf{Q}(\boldsymbol\theta)\mathbf{v}$, whose
gradient is identically zero on every $\boldsymbol\gamma$ coordinate, leaving
two numbers per column:

$$
\text{trace contribution to }\theta_k
= -\tfrac12\,\mathbf{v}^\top\frac{\partial\mathbf{Q}}{\partial\theta_k}\mathbf{v}.
$$

Only first derivatives of the coefficient map are needed for this, and the
result is exactly zero on all $n$ gamma coordinates — a strong invariant, and
one the tests assert directly.

Because $\mathbf{v}$ is sparse, `trace_hinv_t` in the shard stamps
$\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{v})$ and visits only the pattern entries whose row
and column are both stamped, so the per-column cost is
$O(\sum_{c\,\in\,\mathrm{supp}}\mathrm{nnz}(\mathbf{Q}_{\cdot c}))$ rather than
$O(n)$. Every upper-triangle pair $(r,c)$ with $r \le c$ lives in CSC column
$c$, so iterating stamped columns and testing row stamps visits each pair
exactly once.

# What this replaces

Taping the quadratic form puts one multiply-add chain on the AD tape per nonzero
of $\mathbf{Q}$, and three consumers then sweep it.

| Quantity | AD tape path | Closed form |
|---|---|---|
| Value | `Forward(0)` | one fused pass for all $q_j$ |
| Gradient | `Forward(0)` + `Reverse(1)` | one extra sparse matvec |
| Hessian | `Forward(1)`/`Reverse(2)` **per color**; the color count is the distance-2 chromatic number of $\mathbf{Q}$'s graph, in the hundreds for this stencil | copy $\mathbf{Q}$ values, $O(\mathrm{nnz})$ |
| Trace | `Forward(0,1,2)` + `Reverse(3)` **per assigned gamma column**, and every gamma column is assigned to this shard | $O(\lvert\mathrm{supp}\rvert)$ per column, two scalars out |
| Build | record the tape, then four calibration sweeps including the symmetric Hessian coloring | patterns constructed directly, no tape |

The trace row is likely the largest single per-iteration cost in a taped fit,
ahead of even the Hessian coloring. The build row accounts for most of the long
pause with no output before `optim()` starts on a large mesh.

Two points are worth separating, because they explain why this is a shard rather
than a CppAD atomic. First, the Hessian and trace losses happen in CppAD's
*drivers* — `sparse_hes` recovers Hessian values by probing with directional
derivatives, and `EvalShard::trace_hinv_t` clears and fills a dense direction
vector of length $n$ once per column. An atomic sits underneath both and cannot
remove either, because `atomic_four` exposes forward and reverse products but no
hook for handing over sparse Hessian values. Second, an atomic for this term
would have domain $n+2$, so every call marshals dense vectors of that length.
Replacing the shard is the level at which both costs disappear.

# Storage and the three primitives

All $m$ Gram matrices share one sparsity pattern — the upper triangle of
$\mathbf{Q}$ in CSC form, from `fem_precision_payload()`. `femssq::Data` holds
that pattern once (`Q_p`, `Q_i`) plus $m$ aligned value vectors in `M`, along
with per-entry symmetry weights `w` (1 on the diagonal, 2 off it) so that a
single pass over the stored upper triangle yields a full symmetric quadratic
form.

Three primitives in `fem_ssq_analytic.hpp` do all the linear algebra:

| Primitive | Computes | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `combine(d, coef, out)` | `out[k]` $=\sum_j$ `coef[j] * M[j][k]` | assembling $\mathbf{Q}$ and each $\partial\mathbf{Q}/\partial\theta_k$ |
| `sym_matvec(d, A, x, y)` | $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ for symmetric $\mathbf{A}$ in upper-triangle CSC | $-\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\gamma$ and the cross Hessian blocks |
| `sym_quad_all(d, x, out)` | `out[j]` $=\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{M}_j\mathbf{x}$ for all $j$ | the $m$ scalars $q_j$, in one pass |

`sym_quad_all` is fused over $j$ on purpose: the pattern traversal and the
$w_k x_r x_c$ product are shared across all $m$ Grams, so computing all $m$
quadratic forms costs barely more than computing one.

`sym_matvec` accumulates the mirrored contribution separately from the direct
one, so a diagonal entry is not counted twice.

# Per-evaluation state

`femssq::Workspace` holds everything that changes with the parameters:
coefficient values and derivatives (`c`, `dc`, `d2c`), the combined value
vectors (`Q_x`, `dQ_x[k]`), and the derived vectors (`gamma`, `Qg`, `dQg[k]`,
`quad`). `update_theta()` takes an `order` argument so each entry point pays
only for what it needs — order 0 for the value, 1 to add $\partial
c/\partial\theta$ and $\partial\mathbf{Q}/\partial\theta_k$, 2 to add
$\partial^2 c/\partial\theta^2$.

The `trace_hinv_t` scratch deserves a note. Instead of clearing an
$n$-vector per column, the workspace keeps `v_dense` alongside a `stamp` array
and an integer `stamp_tag`; a row counts only when its stamp matches the current
tag, so stale values are never read and nothing needs zeroing.

# Where AD survives

One piece is still automatic differentiation, and correctly so. The map
$\boldsymbol\theta\mapsto\mathbf{c}$ is recorded as a `CppAD::ADFun<double>`
with domain 2 and range $m$ (`make_fem_coef_fun<Alpha>()`), and `update_theta`
calls `Forward`, `Jacobian`, and $m$ tiny `Hessian` calls on it. This avoids
hand-differentiating the $(\mathrm{range},\mathrm{sd}) \to (\kappa,\tau)$
composition together with the optional log transform — four cases, all easy to
get subtly wrong — and it costs nothing next to the $O(m\cdot\mathrm{nnz})$
combine passes.

This is the same principle that makes the log-determinant a good atomic: AD is
cheap and reliable on a two-dimensional domain. It is expensive on an
$n$-dimensional one. The design applies AD exactly where the domain is small.

Because CppAD sweeps are not thread safe, each shard clone takes its own copy of
this tape in `Workspace::init`, so threads never share one.

# Wiring into adlaplace

`ad_shard` is a virtual interface, and `adlaplaceFem` already owns the shard
factory through `ADLAPLACE_DEFINE_BACKEND()`. `FemSsqShard` derives from
`ad_shard` and overrides the evaluation methods; the whole change is contained
in `adlaplaceFem`, with no ABI bump.

| Method | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `f` | $q_j$ pass, then $-\tfrac12\sum_j c_j q_j$ |
| `f_grad` | adds one `sym_matvec` for $-\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\gamma$ |
| `f_grad_hess` | adds `sym_matvec` per $\theta_k$, then fills Hessian nonzeros from slot maps |
| `trace_hinv_t` | stamped support loop, two scalars scattered to the theta slots |
| `get_sizes`, `get_sparse_pattern` | delegate to the free helpers `pack_sparsity_sizes` / `get_pattern` |
| `assign_memory` | nothing to do: no sweeps means no Taylor workspace |
| `clone` | copies the `shared_ptr` to the immutable data |

The bookkeeping that connects closed-form values to the pack's sparsity
patterns is the one genuinely fiddly part. At construction the shard classifies
every nonzero of the four patterns it was handed:

- `GradSlots` marks each gradient nonzero as a gamma row, a theta index, or
  ignorable.
- `HesSlots` marks each Hessian nonzero as `kGammaGamma` (carrying a position
  into `Q_i`), `kGammaTheta` (a gamma row and a theta index), `kThetaTheta`, or
  `kIgnore`.

These are built by reading `pack.pattern_grad`, `pattern_grad_inner`,
`pattern_hessian`, and `pattern_hessian_inner` directly, so the nonzero ordering
is correct by construction rather than by assuming how the analytic pattern
happened to be enumerated.

Two conventions must match `EvalShard` exactly, and they differ from each other:

- `out_f` and `out_grad` are **accumulated** with `+=`, since several shards
  contribute to the same slots.
- `out_hes[map[D]]` is **assigned** with `=`. Structurally present entries whose
  analytic value is zero must therefore be written as explicit zeros rather than
  skipped, which is what the `kIgnore` branch does.

# Two modes

Because the closed forms are worth trusting only if they are checked, the
density keeps an AD reference path behind one config flag.

| `fem_analytic` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `TRUE` (default) | Closed-form `FemSsqShard` evaluation; tape never recorded. |
| `FALSE` | Standard `EvalShard` over a CppAD tape that evaluates $\gamma^\top M_j\gamma$ with `quadform_atomic` (one call per Gram). |

In the default mode `get_tape_sizes()` reports `domain`, `size_op`, and
`size_var` as zero. That is a diagnostic only; nothing downstream consumes it,
and the zeros do not indicate a broken pack.

# Verification

A small model, built both ways from the same FEM ingredients.

```{r pack}
ssq_pack <- function(alpha = 2L, analytic = TRUE,
                     range = sqrt(8) / 1.5, sd = 0.8, nk = 4L) {
  degree <- if (alpha == 2L) 2L else 3L
  knots_list <- list(
    x = seq(0, 1, length.out = nk),
    y = seq(0, 1, length.out = nk)
  )
  sites <- do.call(expand.grid, knots_list)
  fem <- fem_bspline(sites, knots_list, degree = degree)
  prec <- fem_precision_payload(fem, alpha = alpha)
  nr <- nrow(fem$C)

  config <- list(
    gamma = rep(0, nr),
    theta = c(log(range), log(sd)),
    transform_theta = TRUE,
    fem_analytic = analytic
  )
  dd <- adlaplace::density_data(
    gamma_map = Matrix::Diagonal(nr),
    theta_map = list(c(1L, 2L), 2L),
    ad_kind = "random",
    density = paste0("random_fem_ssq_", alpha),
    package = "adlaplaceFem",
    precision = prec
  )
  list(
    ptr = adlaplace::ad_pack_ptr(dd, config),
    fem = fem,
    n_gamma = nr,
    theta = c(log(range), log(sd))
  )
}

analytic <- ssq_pack(analytic = TRUE)
ad <- ssq_pack(analytic = FALSE)

c(n_gamma = analytic$n_gamma)
```

The default mode records no tape, while the patterns match the ones the
atomic AD tape discovers:

```{r tape-sizes}
rbind(
  analytic = unlist(adlaplace:::get_tape_sizes(analytic$ptr, 0L)),
  ad = unlist(adlaplace:::get_tape_sizes(ad$ptr, 0L))
)
```

`domain` and `size_op` collapse to zero on the analytic pack, but `nnz_grad`
and `nnz_hes` agree. The AD tape domain is $n+2$ with a small operator count
from the Gram atomics rather than an $O(\mathrm{nnz}(Q))$ product loop.

Both modes agree on the value, gradient, and Hessian:

```{r agree}
set.seed(3)
x <- c(rnorm(analytic$n_gamma), analytic$theta)

f_of <- function(p) adlaplace::joint_log_dens(p$ptr, x, negative = FALSE)
g_of <- function(p, inner) {
  as.numeric(adlaplace::grad(p$ptr, x, inner = inner, negative = FALSE))
}
H_of <- function(p, inner) {
  as.matrix(adlaplace::hessian(p$ptr, x, inner = inner, negative = FALSE))
}

data.frame(
  quantity = c("log density", "gradient (outer)", "Hessian (outer)"),
  analytic_vs_AD = c(
    abs(f_of(analytic) - f_of(ad)),
    max(abs(g_of(analytic, FALSE) - g_of(ad, FALSE))),
    max(abs(H_of(analytic, FALSE) - H_of(ad, FALSE)))
  )
)
```

The sharpest single check is the identity
$\partial^2 f/\partial\boldsymbol\gamma\partial\boldsymbol\gamma^\top = -\mathbf{Q}$.
Assembling $\mathbf{Q}$ independently in R from $\kappa$ and $\tau$ must
reproduce the gamma block of the inner Hessian exactly, at any
$\boldsymbol\gamma$:

```{r minus-Q}
kappa <- 1.5
sd <- 0.8
tau <- 1 / (kappa * sd * sqrt(4 * pi))
nr <- analytic$n_gamma

H_inner <- H_of(analytic, TRUE)
Q <- as.matrix(fem_precision(
  kappa = kappa, tau = tau,
  analytic$fem$C, analytic$fem$G, analytic$fem$G2,
  alpha = 2L
))

c(max_abs_diff = max(abs(H_inner[seq_len(nr), seq_len(nr)] + Q)))
```

Finally the third-order trace. Both modes agree, and the analytic result is
exactly zero on every gamma coordinate:

```{r trace}
af_analytic <- adlaplace::ad_pack(analytic$ptr, num_threads = 1L)
af_ad <- adlaplace::ad_pack(ad$ptr, num_threads = 1L)

half <- af_analytic@chol_inner_list$half_H_inv
half <- methods::as(methods::as(half, "generalMatrix"), "CsparseMatrix")
set.seed(5)
half@x[] <- rnorm(length(half@x))
cols <- af_analytic@chol_inner_list$trace_columns

t_analytic <- adlaplace::trace_hinv_t(af_analytic, x, half, cols)
t_ad <- adlaplace::trace_hinv_t(af_ad, x, half, cols)

c(
  rel_diff_vs_AD = max(abs(t_analytic - t_ad)) / max(abs(t_ad)),
  max_abs_on_gamma = max(abs(t_analytic[seq_len(nr)])),
  theta_1 = t_analytic[nr + 1L],
  theta_2 = t_analytic[nr + 2L]
)
```

The two theta entries are the whole contribution; the gamma entries are
structurally zero rather than numerically small.

`tests/testthat/test-fem-ssq-analytic.R` runs these comparisons across
$\alpha \in \{2,3\}$ crossed with `transform_theta`, adds the pattern-equality
assertion between the hand-built and tape-discovered patterns, and exercises a
clone under OpenMP.

# Why the log-determinant is an atomic instead

The two FEM terms illustrate the two available extension points, and the choice
between them turns on the size of the domain.

| | `random_fem_det_*` | `random_fem_ssq_*` (analytic) | `random_fem_ssq_*` (AD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | `CppAD::atomic_four` | custom `ad_shard` | `quadform_atomic` on a tape |
| Domain of the hand-written code | $m = 3$ or $4$ coefficients | $n+2$ parameters | fixed Grams; $n$ on each atomic call |
| Derivative route | trace identity $\mathrm{d}\log\det\mathbf{Q} = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Q})$, evaluated with a sparse LDL and a Takahashi selected inverse | direct differentiation of a quadratic form | atomic forward/reverse of $\gamma^\top M_j\gamma$, then chain through $c_j(\theta)$ |
| Highest order implemented | reverse order 1 | closed form throughout | Taylor / reverse through order 2 |
| Sits on a tape | yes | no | yes |

The determinant is a natural atomic because the coefficients are the only
inputs: it is called with a 3- or 4-vector, CppAD's sparsity and coloring
machinery sees a $2\times2$ Hessian, and the atomic can decline orders above 1
outright — which it does. It gets away with that because `trace_columns_from_pattern`
assigns trace columns by matching a shard's `grad_inner` against the gamma
slots, and the determinant depends on $\boldsymbol\theta$ only, so it is never
assigned any.

The quadratic form's production path is the opposite case: it is the term that
gets assigned every gamma column, its Hessian block is an $n\times n$ sparse
matrix, and the expensive structure lives at the shard level. The AD reference
path still uses atomics, but only for the *fixed* Grams $M_j$ (scalar
$y_j = \gamma^\top M_j\gamma$), with $\tau$/range coefficients kept outside —
the same split `random_mult` uses for a fixed $Q$.

One structural precondition makes the analytic shard possible: `random_fem_ssq_*`
is alone in its pack, so the shard can own the entire term. A shard replaces a
whole tape, so if this term ever had to share a tape with others, the atomic AD
path would become the only option.
